<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="ShakespeareFan00" /></noinclude><section begin="par126" />{{GHGmargin-letter|126|i}}
(''i'') On the other hand, the article is always omitted when a person or thing is to be represented as indefinite (or indefinable) or as yet unknown; consequently also before the predicate, since this is from its nature always a general term, under which the subject is included, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=29|verse=7}} {{GHGheb|text=עוֹד הַיּוֹם גָּדוֹל|translate=as yet the day is great}}, i.e. it is yet high day; 33:13, 40:18, 41:26, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=66|verse=3}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|126|k}}
Rem. 1. As exceptions to the above rule it is usual to regard those examples in which a determinate adjective or participle (equivalent to a relative clause) is used apparently as a predicate, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=2|verse=11}} {{GHGheb|text=הוּא הַסֹּבֵב|translate=it is the compassing}}, i.e. ''that is it which compasseth''; 42:6, 45:12, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=9|verse=27}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=3|verse=21}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=8|verse=18|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=11|verse=7|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=4|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=14|verse=27}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mal|chapter=3|verse=2}} (cf. in Greek, e.g. St. Mat. 10:20, where Winer, ''Gram. des neutest. Sprachidioms'', § 58, 2, Rem., explains οἱ λαλοῦντες as a predicate with the article). In reality, however, these supposed predicates are rather subjects (acc. to {{GHGpar|116|q}}), and the only peculiarity of these cases is that the subject is not included under a general idea, but is equated with the predicate.

2. Sometimes the article is used with only one of two parallel words, as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Na|chapter=1|verse=5}} {{GHGheb|text=הָרִים}} and {{GHGheb|text=הַגְּבָעוֹת}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=3|verse=17}} {{GHGheb|text=מִיָּמִין}} and {{GHGheb|text=מֵֽהַשְּׂמֹאול}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|126|l}}
'''3.''' The use of the article to determine the ''class'' is more extensive in Hebrew than in most other languages. In this case the article indicates universally known, closely circumscribed, and therefore well defined classes of persons or things. The special cases to be considered are—

{{GHGmargin-letter|126|m}}
(''a'') The employment of general names as collectives in the singular, to denote the ''sum total'' of individuals belonging to the class (which may, however, be done just as well by the plural); e.g. ''the righteous, the wicked man'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ec|chapter=3|verse=17}}; ''the woman'', i.e. ''the female sex'', 7:26; {{GHGheb|text=הָֽאֹיֵב|translate=the enemy}}, i.e. ''the enemies'' (?) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=9|verse=7}}; {{GHGheb|text=הָֽאֹרֵב|translate=the lier in wait}}, i.e. ''the liers in wait''; {{GHGheb|text=הֶֽחָלוּץ|translate=the armed man}}, i.e. ''soldiers''; {{GHGheb|text=הַֽמְאַסֵּף|translate=the rearguard}}; {{GHGheb|text=הַמַּשְׁחִית|translate=the spoiler}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=13|verse=17}};<ref>But in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=12|verse=23}} {{GHGheb|text=המ׳}} is either to be explained as ''the destroyer'' (now mentioned for the first time) according to ''q'', or a particular angel is meant whose regular function it was to inflict punishments. Others again take {{GHGheb|text=המ׳}} even in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=12|verse=23}} impersonally = ''destruction''.</ref> so also (as in English) with names of animals, when something is asserted of them, which applies to the whole species, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=17|verse=10}} ''as the courage of'' {{GHGheb|text=הָֽאַרְיֵה|translate=the lion}}. Especially also with gentilic names, e.g. ''the Canaanite'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=13|verse=7}} (cf. 15:19<sup> f.</sup>); so in English ''the Russian, the Turk'', &c., in Attic writers ὁ Ἀθηναῖος, ὁ Συρακόσιος, &c.

{{GHGmargin-letter|126|n}}
(''b'') Names of materials known everywhere, the elements and other words denoting classes, even though only a part and not the whole of them is considered, in which case in other languages, as e.g. in English, the article is usually omitted (cf., however, our ''to fall into the water, into the fire'', &c.), e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=13|verse=2}} ''and Abram was very rich'' {{GHGheb|text=בַּמִּקְנֶה בַּכֶּסֶף וּבַזָּהָב|translate=in cattle, in silver and in gold}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jos|chapter=11|verse=9}} ''and he burnt their chariots'' {{GHGheb|text=בָּאֵשׁ|translate=with fire}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=6|verse=14}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=41|verse=42|hidebook=1}} (unless this means, ''the chain'' necessarily belonging to the official dress); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=2|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=31|verse=4|hidebook=1}} (35:32), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=1|verse=22}}, &c., and {{GHGheb|text=בַּשָּׁמֶן|translate=with oil}}<ref>In nearly all the above examples the presence of the article is only indicated by the vowel of the prefix ({{GHGheb|text=בַּ}}, {{GHGheb|text=כַּ‍}}, {{GHGheb|text=לַ}}) and might therefore be merely due to the masoretic punctuation. There is, however, no reason to doubt the correctness of the tradition. The same is true of the examples under ''n'' and ''o''.</ref> very commonly in the sacrificial laws, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=29|verse=2}},<section end="par126" /><noinclude>
